question: Are Luna Peak's Southeast Slopes and Southwest Ridge rows one climb or two?
answer: One climb. Every fetched source describes a single standard route, named the Southwest Ridge: Access Creek, a col at the head of the creek (about 5,800-6,100 ft), a traverse to Luna Col (the Luna/McMillan col), then the southwest ridge, about 1,000 ft of class 3 scrambling over a lower false (south) summit, then an exposed step to the higher true summit. No source names a distinct Southeast Slopes line. Our Southeast Slopes row's own text is that same route (Access Creek, a col, Luna Col, a talus ridge to the false summit, a 5-ft exposed downclimb to the true summit) and its beta even says traverse to southwest ridge. The southeast label comes from the sun-facing basin/shoulder on the way to the col, not a separate line. The Southwest Ridge row's approach/descent text (cairn 1.5 mi past Luna Camp, ford Big Beaver Creek, Access Creek meadows near 4200 ft, 2000 ft loose gully to the col, ramps on the SE side to the false summit, class 3 rock of the SW ridge) is the same route from a guidebook-style source. The 3 logged tracks top out at 48.8310,-121.2719 (the peak) and carry no logged route name, so they do not separate the two. No different first ascent or named variant exists (FA 1938 Cox/Thompson, one route).
recommendation: Merge. Keep wa_luna_peak_southwest_ridge as the surviving row (the name every source uses; it is currently an empty shell so nothing is lost) and move the Southeast Slopes row's content, waypoints, trailhead and 4-point track data into it; then drop wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes. Equivalent alternative: keep the Southeast Slopes id and rename it Southwest Ridge. Either way ONE row named Southwest Ridge. Discipline: not alpine (no 5.x); class 3 with one exposed step = scrambling (Beckey notes some class 4; some parties carry a rope for the step, say so). Grade Class 3. Season Jul-Sep (late July to September best). Fix face/aspect from 'Southeast basin/shoulder'/SE to the ridge: aspect SW. Peak elevation: lidar 8,290 ft; older maps 8,311 ft.
